title: Selling Christmas trees and rotten fish
summary: Stories of buying produce, Christmas trees and a load of bad fish.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And I used to sell Christmas trees. See, I'd sell somewhere around two or three thousand Christmas trees. And when everybody else was busted on Christmas day, I'm sitting there with eight or nine hundred dollars. See? I'd go out there, a lot of times I'd look and go out there in the freight yards. Sometimes a guy had a whole boxcar of Christmas trees. He's cold, you know? And they'd go in kind of slow and something like that. I bought a whole truck of trees and give a guy fifteen dollars. He wanted me to take more because of the contract to enter that boxcar, you know? And so I was taking as much as I could haul. And so I got me about five guys. I told them, say, now go for yourself. All I want is a little money out of this. I'd set one down, maybe a hundred and fifty trees here and go maybe four or five more blocks. Set him down to a hundred and fifty. And so I didn't expect to get as much money as I would if I was selling them myself. I know they're going to cheat me, you know? But I made out of all them trees, I made about four hundred dollars out of them. Because we had some pines, you know? And it had them like this, you know? I sold them pines for two dollars, two and a half. Yeah, and it was sold for two and a half. So we cleaned up all them trees and made some nice money. I'd go down there and get some tomatoes. Sometimes they'd have a skew of tomatoes almost high as a light. Well, you can tell that when something bad and you put your hand under the box, it's damp. So that tells you that there's somebody in there bleeding, you know? And so I had a large garage, I'd take them, same way grapes. It's an old scale of grapes, a quarter of a box. And tomatoes would sell them thirty-five cents a pound. You take and get you some water and wash them off and get rid of the rotten ones, you know? Or you go out there and sell them. You can sell them two pounds for a quarter. You know, you're getting twenty pounds of grapes for a quarter, you understand? You understood you're getting some rotten ones. You know, I'm going to tell you this and I guess it'll be finished. This is a funny thing. A friend of mine said, Jack, he called me Jack, right on there, see? Not Preston Jack. Jack, why don't you hunt them fish? I said, I believe I will, Joe. So Joe carried me to this market. There's three of them. I'm going to put them in one direction, one here and one diagonal and one in the next corner on Fulton Street. A guy gave me 280 pounds of fish for seventeen dollars. So I'd already been to the market. I bought me some tomatoes and lettuce and things to go with these fish. It was on a Friday. And so on the way back to the garage, that fish began to hit me in the nose, you know? I said, my uncle's name was Cookie. I said, Cookie? I said, you smell what I smell? He said, you're damn right. He said, look like we got some rotten fish. I said, oh boy. I said, it must be rotten. I said, mm-hmm. So we went off the garage and we was pondering what to do with the fish. I hate to lose my seventeen dollars and don't have a load either. It's too late for me to go pick up a load at the market. So I said, well, I'll just reimburse the people as they catch me tomorrow. Saturday's my best day. So we had a tub of water, warm water. We had soap. We had steel and good knives and clean towels and everything. I sold $22 away from fish before I moved from the garage. And I didn't want to sell those people. It was my neighbors. I didn't want to sell them any, but I had to come to the garage. So I said, oh Lord, I'm dead. So we made our rounds and sold all that fish. But I still could smell that fish. So the next day around, the people said, oh my goodness, Mr. Jackson. Where'd you get that nice fish? I said, well, I'll go now. So anyhow, I wouldn't go back to the same bar and buy a fish. I knew I'd say today that that fish was rotten. I wouldn't go back to him. I went to another place. I got Lake Superior. I got push. I got catfish. It was high. Catfish was about 80 cents a pound then, see. And Joe went back and got 400 some pounds of fish. He had two trucks. And he bought 400 pounds and had to give the people the money back. Yeah. I'd lose all these customers. How did you make out in the 50s with Natty Dominic and Baby and Baby and Baby? I knew, man, something was wrong with that fish. See, I wouldn't go back. He'd say, you sure a smart guy. You a smart guy. See, I told him, I said, Joe. I said, Joe, I sold all that fish, but there's something wrong with that fish smell. That stink like that. And Joe went back and bought another load and had to give the people all the money back. Yeah. Or lose all these customers.
